title: Voyager 1 Reaches a Light-Day From Earth
summary: On November 18, Voyager 1 will be so far from Earth that a radio signal will take a full day, 24 hours, to reach it. That distance is called a light-day: about 16,094,799,096 miles from home. NASA is asking fans to shine Morse code signals at the sky to celebrate. Its twin, Voyager 2, will not reach the same mark until about 2035, nearly ten years later. Voyager 2 launched first in 1977, and Voyager 1 followed about two weeks later on a faster path, reaching Jupiter four months before Voyager 2. Both used a gravity assist, a slingshot around a planet that borrows a little of its speed to go faster while saving fuel, gaining about 10 kilometers per second at Jupiter. Voyager 1 then turned at Saturn to study Saturn's rings and its moon Titan. Voyager 2 kept going to Uranus and Neptune, but it lost about 2 kilometers per second at Neptune. Today Voyager 1 travels at 3.5 Earth-sun distances a year, and Voyager 2 at 3.1. Both have left the solar system, Voyager 1 in 2012 and Voyager 2 in 2018, and they may keep working into the 2030s while their nuclear power lasts.
why_it_matters: Knowing how far spacecraft can travel helps us dream about exploring space ourselves one day.

background_read: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 are twin space probes that NASA sent out to explore the planets far from Earth.
They used a gravity assist, swinging around giant planets to borrow speed and save fuel, so they could travel farther than ever before.
After passing the planets, both probes kept flying outward and crossed the edge of the solar system into the space between the stars.
Article_Structure: WHO: NASA's twin space probes, Voyager 1 and Voyager 2.
WHAT: Voyager 1 reaches a distance from Earth so far that a radio signal takes a full day to reach it.
WHERE: Deep space, far beyond the planets of the solar system.
WHY: To mark how far the twin probes have traveled since they launched in 1977 and to celebrate their long journey.
